name: Rangkhol
confidence_why: The only statement on Rangkhol word stress is Soppitt's 1887 outline grammar, which gives initial stress that moves to the final syllable in compounds and inflected nouns and with sentence emphasis, while the modern first-hand descriptions, Debbarma 2018 and Haokip 2021, treat Hrangkhol as a tone language and say nothing about stress, so the record rests on one pre-modern source that nothing confirms.

new_statements.quote: Word stems in the KC languages of Barak valley are both monosyllabic and disyllabic. Monosyllabic stems consist of a single major syllable. Disyallabic stems, on the other hand, often consist of a prefix followed by the main syllable; commonly known as sesquisyllables in the literature on Tibeto-Burman language study. This pattern is consistent with a general tendency towards right-handed (iambic) prosodic constituents. The minor syllable is unstressed and the vowels are never long compared to stressed syllables which are louder than unstressed syllables, and pitch excursions are more pronounced in stressed syllables.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record for Rangkhol has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this work supplies the first usable statement: tonal, sesquisyllabic/iambic with unstressed minor (initial) syllable and stressed final major syllable. Compatible with (adds detail to) the empty catalog entry. How opened: live academia.edu blocked (2 automated download attempts, not reachable by automated download an automated-access block); the Internet Archive 2025-07-09 snapshot = abstract/captions only; the Internet Archive's index shows no PDF capture; the Internet Archive 2022-11-10 snapshot of the same page carries the full extracted text (pp. 85-114 with running heads) and was read.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hrangkhol (with the other Barak Valley Kuki-Chin languages) is a lexical tone language (H, HL, L; tone inventory conditioned by syllable type, Hrangkhol CVVD syllables carry only HL and L, sec. 4.3.2 p. 109f). Words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic; prosodic constituents are right-headed (iambic): the prefixal minor syllable (Cə-, reduced pronominal clitics, sə-/mə-/rə-) is unstressed, toneless (takes its tone from the major syllable) and never long, while the final major syllable is stressed (louder, larger pitch excursions). I.e. stem-/word-final prominence in disyllables; no independent contrastive stress is described.
new_statements.exceptions: None as exceptions to placement. Related detail: p. 91 (sec. 2.2) vowel length is contrastive 'except in open syllables where the vowel naturally surfaces as long unless occurring as the unstressed initial syllable of a disyllabic compound'; p. 99 'The minor syllables in themselves do not carry any tone of their own, but received tone from the corresponding main syllables.'
new_statements.identity_note: Haokip describes Hrangkhol (ISO 639-3 hra; Grierson's spelling 'Rangkhol' = Glottolog hran1239) as spoken by c. 7000-8000 people in Karimganj and Dima Hasao districts of Assam (Barak Valley), data collected 2012-2014 from speakers Labiak Phoitong and Pachung Hrangkhol. The stress/prosodic-constituent statements in sec. 3.1 are made jointly for all five Barak Valley Kuki-Chin languages (Saihriem, Hrangkhol, Ranglong, Chorei, Sakachep), not for Hrangkhol individually; the Hrangkhol-specific content is the tone inventories by syllable type (sec. 4) and the segmental inventories (sec. 2). The Tripura variety (Hrangkhawl, Debbarma 2018) is a different dialect and is not the object of this paper.

new_statements.quote: (p. 91) Five vowels and two diphthongs are generally regular across the five KC languages of Barak valley. These vowels show distinctive length except in open syllables where the vowel naturally surfaces as long unless occurring as the unstressed initial syllable of a disyllabic compound. ... (p. 102) Like other KC languages, Barak valley KC tone is largely determined by syllable types. The nature of tone is examined in major syllable types viz. CVT, CVVT, CVD and CVVD. ... (p. 109) CVVD syllable is associated with different tones. Saihriem and Ranglong show three tones (HL, LH, and L), while Hrangkhol has only two tones (HL and L)

tone.quote: Our information with regard to tones in the Kuki-Chin languages is very defective. Sho is said to possess three tones — the short acute, the heavy grave, and the rising tones ; two tones, the light and heavy one, are mentioned in Khami ; and the abrupt shortening of a syllable in Lushei seems to indicate the existence of the short abrupt tone in that language.

sources.note: The only dedicated modern phonetics/phonology of Hrangkhol (28 pp, from a phonetics lab; the volume foreword promises tone-phoneme descriptions with minimal pairs for every language). Our 'variable stress' coding rests solely on an 1887 colonial outline grammar; this chapter would show whether any word-stress/prominence statement exists alongside the tone system, or whether the language is described as tone-only (which would put tonal-OR-pitch accent on the table).
